newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: SECOND ALICE SPRINGS YACHT REACHES HOBART
In the Sydney to Hobart race, the second entry from the Alice Springs yacht club was one of the overnight finishers, as the tail end of the fleet continues to arrive.
The Alice was joined at the Hobart docks by Tasmanian yacht Interim and Suraya from Sydney.
Thirty-eight boats have now finished the race, with eighteen still to cross the line.
Organisers say most of the remaining yachts are in the Tasman sea, facing light winds.
LAW NOT MEDIA TO BLAME: NITSCHKE
Darwin doctor Phillip Nitshcke says the complexities of the voluntary euthanasia law, not the media, is to blame for the legislation being unworkable.
South Australian woman Janet Mills wants to use the law, and has secured two of the neccesary doctors signatures but is unable to find a willing Territory specialist for the third.
Yesterday Northern Territory Chief Minister, Shane Stone, said the media was to blame for doctors being reluctant to come forward and support the law.
But Dr Nitshcke says specialist doctors are hostile to the legislation and have sewn into the act, the seeds of its destruction.
NT ATTORNEY SLATES WIK RULING
The Northern Territory Attorney General, Denis Burke, says the High Court's Wik ruling has turned the basis of the Mabo decision on its head.
Mr Burke says the ruling means pastoral leases don't extinguish Native Title even though the former Federal government said they did.

He says the Mabo decision was based on the premise that Native Title existed only for those indigenous people who have not been dispossessed, but the Wik decision says those who feel possession can claim it in retrospect.
Mr Burke says the Wik ruling has retarded the progress of land rights in Australia by three years, because it changes the rules by which State and Territory Governments have been working.
NEW YEAR'S EVE PARTY PREPARATIONS
Australia's capital cities and many holiday spots are gearing up for New Year's Eve celebrations tonight.
Police are warning they won't put up with trouble-makers, and revellers are being urged to use public transport, rather than drinking and driving.
In Sydney, police will be out in record numbers with about six hundred officers in the CBD and two hundred at Bondi Beach, where there'll be an organised party.
Some city roads will be closed during a firworks display on Sydney harbour.
In Adelaide, Jimmy Barnes will perform at the Alberton Oval and there'll be parties at the Adelaide Town Hall and Glenelg.
Extra taxis and free public transport will operate in some centres.
LEUKAEMIA CASES ON GOLD COAST
Health officials in Queensland are trying to find out why eight cases on leukaemia have been reported from an area on the Gold Coast since June.
The Health Department hopes to complete a study of the cases reported in the Palm Beach-Currumbin area, by the end of next week.
Acting Chief Health Officer, Doctor John Youngman, says the leukaemia cases differ and it's too early to say whether they represent a cluster or are linked to environmental factors.
Hospitals and private doctors are being asked for details of all leukaemia cases in the area concerned, while the eight cases reported are investigated.
